From analyticsto data science.

I’m a data and analytics professional with several years of experience in analytics and business intelligence, working with international clients. I’m currently pursuing a Master of Data Science at the University of British Columbia, where I’m strengthening my skills in data science, machine learning, and analytical problem-solving. I’m interested in using data to uncover meaningful insights and build practical solutions to real-world problems. Through MDS, I hope to combine my analytics experience with deeper technical expertise.


About Me Blog

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Starting the MDS program at UBC has been an exciting experience so far. The first few weeks have been a mix of orientation, meeting new people, getting familiar with the program, and settling into a new academic routine. It has been interesting to see how quickly the program has brought together people with different backgrounds and experiences.
One of the things that stood out to me was how quickly the pace picked up once classes began. There has already been a lot to learn, particularly around programming, statistics, and working with data. Coming from an analytics and business intelligence background, I’m looking forward to building on what I already know while developing stronger technical skills.
I’m still getting used to the workload and the rhythm of MDS, but I’m enjoying the challenge. I’m especially excited to see how the concepts we learn in class connect to real-world data problems and to the work I hope to do in the future.

title: Exploring Iris Flower Measurements
text:
In this post, I use R to explore measurements of three species of iris flowers. The dataset contains measurements of sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width.
The goal is to explore the measurements, calculate average petal length by species, and visualize the differences between species.
Data source: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/iris.html

title: Exploring Iris Flower Measurements
text:
In this post, I use R to explore measurements of three species of iris flowers. The dataset contains measurements of sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width.
The goal is to explore the measurements, calculate average petal length by species, and visualize the differences between species.
Data source: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/iris.html

title: Exploring Iris Flower Measurements
text:
Loading the data
First, I load the built-in iris dataset in R.
#| message: false #| warning: false
data(iris)
head(iris) The dataset contains 150 observations and measurements for three iris species.
Exploring the data
Next, I check the structure of the dataset and examine the number of observations for each species.
str(iris)
table(iris$Species)
This confirms that the dataset contains three iris species with 50 observations for each species.
Comparing average petal length
Next, I calculate the average petal length for each species.
average_petal_length <- aggregate( Petal.Length ~ Species, data = iris, FUN = mean )
average_petal_length
The resulting table shows the average petal length for each iris species.
Visualizing petal length
Finally, I create a boxplot to compare petal length across the three species.
#| label: fig-petal-length #| fig-cap: “Petal length measurements across iris species.”
boxplot( Petal.Length ~ Species, data = iris, xlab = “Iris species”, ylab = “Petal length”, main = “Petal Length by Iris Species” )
The boxplot makes it easier to compare the distribution of petal lengths across the three species.
What I found
The analysis shows that petal length differs across the three iris species. The summary table gives the average petal length for each species, while the boxplot shows the distribution of individual measurements.
This analysis demonstrates how R can be used to load a dataset, explore its structure, calculate grouped summaries, and create a visualization. ’’’

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass
text:
In this post, I use Python to explore body mass differences among penguin species. I use the Palmer Penguins dataset, which contains measurements of penguins from three species.
The goal is to load the data, clean the relevant variables, calculate average body mass by species, and visualize the results.
Data source: Palmer Penguins.

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass
text:
In this post, I use Python to explore body mass differences among penguin species. I use the Palmer Penguins dataset, which contains measurements of penguins from three species.
The goal is to load the data, clean the relevant variables, calculate average body mass by species, and visualize the results.
Data source: Palmer Penguins.

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass
text:
Cleaning the data
Next, I keep the variables needed for this analysis and remove rows with missing species or body mass values.

penguins_clean = penguins[["species", "body_mass_g"]].dropna()

This gives us a clean dataset containing the penguin species and body mass measurements needed for the analysis.

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass
text:
Comparing average body mass
Next, I calculate the average body mass for each penguin species.

average_mass = (
    penguins_clean
    .groupby("species", as_index=False)["body_mass_g"]
    .mean()
    .sort_values("body_mass_g", ascending=False)
)

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass
text:
Visualizing body mass
Finally, I create a bar chart to compare the average body mass across species.

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))

plt.bar(
    average_mass["species"],
    average_mass["body_mass_g"]
)

plt.xlabel("Penguin species")
plt.ylabel("Average body mass (g)")
plt.title("Average Body Mass by Penguin Species")

plt.show()







Figure 1: Average body mass of penguins by species.





The bar chart makes it easier to compare the average body mass of the three penguin species visually.

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass
text:
What I found
The analysis shows that penguin species differ in their average body mass. The bar chart makes these differences easy to compare visually.
This simple analysis demonstrates how Python can be used to load a dataset, clean data, calculate grouped summaries, and create a visualization.

title: From analyticsto data science.
text:
A LITTLE ABOUT ME


From analyticsto data science.

I’m a data and analytics professional with several years of experience in analytics and business intelligence, working with international clients. I’m currently pursuing a Master of Data Science at the University of British Columbia, building on my experience while developing deeper technical skills.




BACKGROUND


My professional journey has been centred around working with data to understand business problems and communicate meaningful insights. Before starting my MDS, I worked in analytics and business intelligence, gaining experience with data, reporting, and analytical problem-solving across international projects.





WHY DATA SCIENCE


Working with data made me want to explore what was possible beyond traditional analytics. I became increasingly interested in using statistics, programming, and machine learning to uncover patterns, make predictions, and build practical solutions. The MDS program is giving me the opportunity to strengthen these skills and move further into data science.





OUTSIDE OF DATA SCIENCE


When I’m not working with data, I enjoy exploring new places, trying different foods, discovering cafés and restaurants, and spending time with friends and family. Since moving to Vancouver, I’ve also enjoyed exploring the city and finding new places to visit on weekends.
